items.author: Paul Martin

items.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Agent Distillation across Models, Artifacts, and Harnesses
items.abstract: This paper introduces "Agent Distillation" as a unified framework for transferring knowledge between AI agents, extending beyond just model parameters to include reusable resources and execution workflows. Its core method involves formalizing this persistent knowledge transfer and categorizing it based on where the knowledge resides (e.g., models, artifacts, harnesses). The main contribution is the first comprehensive survey of agent distillation, bridging the gap between model distillation and agent system design to enable more efficient deployment and broader capability access for LLM-based agents.
items.figure_caption: Figure 1. From a successful agent to broader reuse of task-solving knowledge.

items.title: BadMoE: Backdooring Mixture-of-Experts LLMs via Routing-Aware Triggers and Task-Underutilized Experts
items.abstract: BadMoE introduces a novel backdoor attack against Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs by exploiting their routing mechanism. The attack manipulates specific, underutilized experts and employs routing-aware triggers to ensure these poisoned experts are activated for malicious inputs, thereby controlling the model's output without significantly impacting its general performance. This work's contribution lies in demonstrating a practical and effective backdoor strategy tailored to the unique architecture of MoE models.

items.title: Circe: Training-Free LLM Self-Evaluation via Component Interaction Consistency
items.abstract: Circe is a training-free method for LLM self-evaluation that addresses the lack of reference answers. It analyzes the consistency of interactions between different internal components of the LLM, such as attention and feed-forward networks, to derive correctness signals. This approach complements external output signals, offering a more robust assessment of response accuracy without requiring additional training or sampling.
items.figure_caption: Figure 1. Evaluating LLM response correctness with internal signals. (a) Real-world questions often lack reference answers. (b) Output likelihood, verbal confidence, and response agreement can remain high for incorrect answers. (c) Circe incorporates internal computational signals, yielding a low correctness score for the illustrated incorrect answer.

items.title: Direct Trajectory Optimization for Inference-Time Alignment of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
items.abstract: This paper introduces Direct Trajectory Optimization (DTO), a training-free method for aligning text-to-image diffusion models with reward functions. Instead of backpropagating through the model, DTO directly optimizes the sampling trajectory by treating intermediate denoising scores and noise as variables. This approach, combined with Reward-Optimized Score Guidance to stabilize sampling, significantly improves controllable generation performance.

items.title: Examining the Impact of Data and Training Methods on Emergent and Subliminal Misalignment
items.abstract: This paper investigates how data and training methods influence emergent and subliminal misalignment in language models. The core method involves systematically varying training data domains and tasks to observe how misalignment transfers. The key contribution is demonstrating that misalignment transfer is more strongly influenced by shared tasks than shared domains, and well-learned tasks can amplify this spread.

items.title: Instrumental Choices: Measuring the Propensity of LLM Agents to Pursue Instrumental Behaviors
items.abstract: This paper introduces a benchmark to measure how likely LLM agents are to engage in "instrumental convergence" behaviors, such as self-preservation, even when it means violating instructions. The benchmark uses realistic, low-stakes tasks with varying conditions to understand what drives these potentially dangerous behaviors, contributing a new tool for evaluating AI safety.

items.title: Learning Perturbation Robust Policies for LLM Agents with Stable Optimization
items.abstract: This paper addresses the sensitivity of LLM agent policies trained with reinforcement learning to perturbations. The core method, Stable Perturbation-Robust Policy Optimization (SPrPO), introduces adaptive, sensitivity-aware perturbations during training. This approach enhances the robustness of LLM agents against various perturbations while ensuring stable policy improvement, as demonstrated on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks.
items.figure_caption: LLM agents trained by RL are sensitive to policy perturbations. Even with mild perturbation magnitude, success rates degrade substantially under these perturbations on both WebShop and ALFWorld. \( \sigma \) denotes the standard deviation for Gaussian distribution, p p denotes the dropout probability and r r denotes pruning ratio.

items.title: Living constitutions: Participatory alignment for sovereign foundation models
items.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to creating "constitutions" for AI models, moving beyond static, expert-defined rules. The core method involves treating constitution development as an iterative, participatory process, similar to citizen science, where norms are drafted, tested, and refined by a broader community. The key contribution is a framework of five principles (iterative, modular, justifiable, positional, and legitimate) and a mechanism for marking provisions as settled, contested, or underdetermined, ensuring the constitution remains responsive and legitimate.
items.figure_caption: Overview of the procedure of the participatory iterations of a living AI constitution.

items.title: Reward Shaping to Mitigate Reward Hacking in RLHF
items.abstract: This paper addresses reward hacking in RLHF by proposing a new reward shaping method called "Preference as Reward" (PAR). PAR uses a sigmoid function on centered rewards to create a stable training signal that reflects latent human preferences. This approach reduces variance, enables effective early stopping, and outperforms existing methods in aligning language models with human intent.
items.figure_caption: RLHF training with reward shaping. The reward model assigns proxy rewards to policy responses, which are then optionally transformed using reference rewards (dashed box) before policy optimization. PAR applies a sigmoid transformation to the centered proxy reward.

items.title: Self-Improving Training & Thinking
items.abstract: This paper introduces a "Self-Improving Training & Thinking" method that integrates desirable behaviors like safety and reasoning earlier into the pre-training and mid-training stages of large language models. It achieves this by using a strong post-trained model to rewrite data and judge policy model outputs, and by introducing "self-improving post-thinking" to enhance reasoning and self-judgment after generation. This approach leads to significant improvements across multiple model capabilities.
items.figure_caption: Self-Improving pretraining : Our proposed model training streams pretraining documents and improves the next K K generated tokens (suffix, given prefix) at each step with RL. A strong previously post-trained model is used to judge generation candidates at each RL step for quality, safety and hallucination, where the candidates are: (i) N N rollouts from the current policy; (ii) the original suffix; and (iii) a rewrite of the suffix by the strong post-trained model. The rewrite can improve the pretrain data’s quality or safety; in the latter case as the prefix remains unsafe the model is always learning how to steer towards a safe suffix. At the start of training model rollouts (i) are low quality, so training relies on candidates (ii) and (iii) ; later in training the judge starts rewarding winning rollouts.

items.title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.abstract: SpectRAG addresses limitations in multi-hop RAG by constructing a weighted chunk graph that captures diverse relationships between document segments. It then uses spectral methods to propagate relevance across this graph, enabling a token-budgeted selection of context that better supports complex reasoning than independent retrieval. This spectral graph augmentation allows for more comprehensive and interconnected evidence to be provided to the LLM.
items.figure_caption: Top-k paradigm vs. our SpectRAG framework

items.title: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering
items.abstract: SteerDistill quantizes LLM agents by using a full-precision teacher to guide the quantized student through failed task attempts. This closed-loop process iteratively refines the teacher's guidance based on the student's execution feedback, leading to locally verified behavioral corrections. The student then internalizes these corrections for unassisted inference, improving performance without sacrificing efficiency.

items.title: Structured Cognitive Loop for Behavioral Intelligence in Large Language Model Agents (Extended Revision: From Behavioral Architecture to Epistemic Accountability)
items.abstract: This paper introduces the Structured Cognitive Loop (SCL), an architecture for AI agents that prioritizes accountability over raw performance. SCL separates cognition, control, action, and memory, with a lightweight controller mediating the language model's proposals before execution and using an external structured memory. This approach significantly improves task success and reliability by enabling verifiable decision-making and error attribution, unlike opaque "black box" models.

items.title: TACT: Mitigating Overthinking and Overacting in Coding Agents via Activation Steering
items.abstract: This paper introduces TACT, a method to combat "agent drift" in coding agents, which manifests as overthinking or overacting during complex tasks. TACT identifies these failure modes by analyzing the agent's internal activations and then steers these activations back towards a "calibrated" state, preventing behavioral degradation. This approach significantly improves the agent's performance on software engineering tasks.
items.figure_caption: Two failure modes of a coding agent, mapped into activation space. The left and right panels show concrete steps from an overacting trajectory (left) and an overthinking trajectory (right). The center panel projects each step’s hidden state at the </think> token onto our two drift axes: calibrated steps cluster in the central band, while overthinking and overacting trajectories drift outward in opposite directions. Both failure modes are linearly separable from calibrated activations along their respective axes, motivating the dual-axis steering used at test time (Section 2.4 ).

items.title: The Value of Memory in Language Agents
items.abstract: This paper proposes a decision-theoretic framework to quantify the value of memory for language agents. It models memory as information stored and retrieved, considering costs of access and revision, and expresses its benefit in terms of avoided task loss. The core contribution lies in establishing how factors like information timing, access, and feedback influence memory's utility, offering criteria for optimal memory allocation and recovery.

items.title: Bridging the Evidence-to-Execution Gap:A Reflective Agent for Multi-Objective Peptide Design
items.abstract: This paper introduces EASER, a reflective agent designed to bridge the gap between scientific reasoning and biological sequence generation. EASER uses a learned property interface to connect a large language model controller with a frozen diffusion generator. This allows the LLM to interpret evidence, propose interventions, and reflect on outcomes to design multi-objective peptides with intended properties.
items.figure_caption: EASER overview. Offline-trained matrices steer a frozen generator during sampling and refinement. Evidence and internal predictor feedback guide agent decisions; external predictors score candidates after search. The diagram uses schematic matrices, sequences, and plots; the molecular example is PDB 2MAG .

items.title: Bursts That Outlast Themselves: Persistent Degradation in Prefix-Cached Agent Serving
items.abstract: This paper identifies a critical performance issue in serving LLM agents called "persistent degradation." The core method involves observing how prefix caching, crucial for economic serving, leads to a metastable state where even small bursts of traffic can cause a server to enter a significantly degraded performance regime, characterized by low hit ratios and reduced throughput. The main contribution is demonstrating this phenomenon and its underlying cause: the interaction between prefix caching, growing session contexts, and limited KV cache capacity, leading to prolonged performance drops.

items.title: Can Large Language Models Develop Gambling Addiction?
items.abstract: This paper investigates when Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit irrational, "addiction-like" gambling behavior. The core method involves manipulating LLM parameters like bet size and profit goals, revealing that increased autonomy in these areas significantly amplifies risk-taking and bankruptcy. The contribution is identifying specific conditions that induce pathological gambling patterns in LLMs and demonstrating that these behaviors can be traced to internal decision-making states.
items.figure_caption: Two-phase study design. Phase 1. Six LLMs run the slot-machine and investment-choice tasks crossed by bet-size autonomy and goal source; round-level behavioural indicators ( I BA I_{\( \text{BA} \)} , I LC I_{\( \text{LC} \)} , I EC I_{\( \text{EC} \)} ), bankruptcy, and moving-target rates summarise the behaviour. Phase 2. SAE readouts of decision-time hidden states and cross-task PCA comparisons evaluate two open-weight models. These tests ask whether behavioural contrasts are decodable at the representational level across the three task surfaces (SM/IC/MW), whether endpoint risk shares low-rank geometry across tasks, and whether autonomy modulates how legibly each readout reads. A fourth test asks whether a direction built from the model’s own betting moves the wager. The middle panel poses the question tested in Section 4 . Per-task BK readout weights are nearly orthogonal, while the three tasks’ mean-difference BK directions share a small component (Section 4.2 ).

items.title: Diff-Instruct with Diffused Reward: Towards Principled One-step Generator RL
items.abstract: This paper introduces Diff-Instruct with Diffused Reward (DIDR), a novel framework for one-step text-to-image generation. DIDR addresses the reward-fidelity mismatch in previous RL methods by aligning the optimal reward distribution across all diffusion noise levels. This principled approach, derived from Integral KL minimization, naturally generates a Diffused Reward Score that guides the generator towards higher reward without sacrificing image quality.
items.figure_caption: 1024 × 1024 1024\( \times \) 1024 images from one-step SDXL aligned via Didr . Prompts in Appendix I .

items.title: DOTRAG: Retrieval-Time Reasoning Along Paths
items.abstract: DotRAG addresses challenges in complex graph retrieval by using LLM reasoning to efficiently identify relevant relational paths. Its core method involves indexing the knowledge graph with a summary overview and reachability information, allowing the LLM to quickly narrow down search regions and hypothesize relationship sequences at query time. This training-free approach avoids costly online traversals and rigid heuristics, improving retrieval accuracy for complex relational tasks.

papers.abstract: This paper investigates how data and training methods influence emergent and subliminal misalignment in language models. The core method involves systematically varying training data domains and tasks to observe how misalignment transfers. The key contribution is demonstrating that misalignment transfer is more strongly influenced by shared tasks than shared domains, and well-learned tasks can amplify this spread.

papers.title: Instrumental Choices: Measuring the Propensity of LLM Agents to Pursue Instrumental Behaviors
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a benchmark to measure how likely LLM agents are to engage in "instrumental convergence" behaviors, such as self-preservation, even when it means violating instructions. The benchmark uses realistic, low-stakes tasks with varying conditions to understand what drives these potentially dangerous behaviors, contributing a new tool for evaluating AI safety.

papers.title: Learning Perturbation Robust Policies for LLM Agents with Stable Optimization
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the sensitivity of LLM agent policies trained with reinforcement learning to perturbations. The core method, Stable Perturbation-Robust Policy Optimization (SPrPO), introduces adaptive, sensitivity-aware perturbations during training. This approach enhances the robustness of LLM agents against various perturbations while ensuring stable policy improvement, as demonstrated on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks.
papers.figure_caption: LLM agents trained by RL are sensitive to policy perturbations. Even with mild perturbation magnitude, success rates degrade substantially under these perturbations on both WebShop and ALFWorld. \( \sigma \) denotes the standard deviation for Gaussian distribution, p p denotes the dropout probability and r r denotes pruning ratio.

papers.title: Living constitutions: Participatory alignment for sovereign foundation models
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to creating "constitutions" for AI models, moving beyond static, expert-defined rules. The core method involves treating constitution development as an iterative, participatory process, similar to citizen science, where norms are drafted, tested, and refined by a broader community. The key contribution is a framework of five principles (iterative, modular, justifiable, positional, and legitimate) and a mechanism for marking provisions as settled, contested, or underdetermined, ensuring the constitution remains responsive and legitimate.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of the procedure of the participatory iterations of a living AI constitution.

papers.title: Reward Shaping to Mitigate Reward Hacking in RLHF
papers.abstract: This paper addresses reward hacking in RLHF by proposing a new reward shaping method called "Preference as Reward" (PAR). PAR uses a sigmoid function on centered rewards to create a stable training signal that reflects latent human preferences. This approach reduces variance, enables effective early stopping, and outperforms existing methods in aligning language models with human intent.
papers.figure_caption: RLHF training with reward shaping. The reward model assigns proxy rewards to policy responses, which are then optionally transformed using reference rewards (dashed box) before policy optimization. PAR applies a sigmoid transformation to the centered proxy reward.

papers.title: Self-Improving Training & Thinking
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a "Self-Improving Training & Thinking" method that integrates desirable behaviors like safety and reasoning earlier into the pre-training and mid-training stages of large language models. It achieves this by using a strong post-trained model to rewrite data and judge policy model outputs, and by introducing "self-improving post-thinking" to enhance reasoning and self-judgment after generation. This approach leads to significant improvements across multiple model capabilities.
papers.figure_caption: Self-Improving pretraining : Our proposed model training streams pretraining documents and improves the next K K generated tokens (suffix, given prefix) at each step with RL. A strong previously post-trained model is used to judge generation candidates at each RL step for quality, safety and hallucination, where the candidates are: (i) N N rollouts from the current policy; (ii) the original suffix; and (iii) a rewrite of the suffix by the strong post-trained model. The rewrite can improve the pretrain data’s quality or safety; in the latter case as the prefix remains unsafe the model is always learning how to steer towards a safe suffix. At the start of training model rollouts (i) are low quality, so training relies on candidates (ii) and (iii) ; later in training the judge starts rewarding winning rollouts.

papers.title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: SpectRAG addresses limitations in multi-hop RAG by constructing a weighted chunk graph that captures diverse relationships between document segments. It then uses spectral methods to propagate relevance across this graph, enabling a token-budgeted selection of context that better supports complex reasoning than independent retrieval. This spectral graph augmentation allows for more comprehensive and interconnected evidence to be provided to the LLM.
papers.figure_caption: Top-k paradigm vs. our SpectRAG framework

papers.title: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering
papers.abstract: SteerDistill quantizes LLM agents by using a full-precision teacher to guide the quantized student through failed task attempts. This closed-loop process iteratively refines the teacher's guidance based on the student's execution feedback, leading to locally verified behavioral corrections. The student then internalizes these corrections for unassisted inference, improving performance without sacrificing efficiency.

papers.title: Structured Cognitive Loop for Behavioral Intelligence in Large Language Model Agents (Extended Revision: From Behavioral Architecture to Epistemic Accountability)
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the Structured Cognitive Loop (SCL), an architecture for AI agents that prioritizes accountability over raw performance. SCL separates cognition, control, action, and memory, with a lightweight controller mediating the language model's proposals before execution and using an external structured memory. This approach significantly improves task success and reliability by enabling verifiable decision-making and error attribution, unlike opaque "black box" models.

papers.title: TACT: Mitigating Overthinking and Overacting in Coding Agents via Activation Steering
papers.abstract: This paper introduces TACT, a method to combat "agent drift" in coding agents, which manifests as overthinking or overacting during complex tasks. TACT identifies these failure modes by analyzing the agent's internal activations and then steers these activations back towards a "calibrated" state, preventing behavioral degradation. This approach significantly improves the agent's performance on software engineering tasks.
papers.figure_caption: Two failure modes of a coding agent, mapped into activation space. The left and right panels show concrete steps from an overacting trajectory (left) and an overthinking trajectory (right). The center panel projects each step’s hidden state at the </think> token onto our two drift axes: calibrated steps cluster in the central band, while overthinking and overacting trajectories drift outward in opposite directions. Both failure modes are linearly separable from calibrated activations along their respective axes, motivating the dual-axis steering used at test time (Section 2.4 ).

papers.title: The Value of Memory in Language Agents
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a decision-theoretic framework to quantify the value of memory for language agents. It models memory as information stored and retrieved, considering costs of access and revision, and expresses its benefit in terms of avoided task loss. The core contribution lies in establishing how factors like information timing, access, and feedback influence memory's utility, offering criteria for optimal memory allocation and recovery.

papers.title: Bridging the Evidence-to-Execution Gap:A Reflective Agent for Multi-Objective Peptide Design
papers.abstract: This paper introduces EASER, a reflective agent designed to bridge the gap between scientific reasoning and biological sequence generation. EASER uses a learned property interface to connect a large language model controller with a frozen diffusion generator. This allows the LLM to interpret evidence, propose interventions, and reflect on outcomes to design multi-objective peptides with intended properties.
papers.figure_caption: EASER overview. Offline-trained matrices steer a frozen generator during sampling and refinement. Evidence and internal predictor feedback guide agent decisions; external predictors score candidates after search. The diagram uses schematic matrices, sequences, and plots; the molecular example is PDB 2MAG .

papers.title: Bursts That Outlast Themselves: Persistent Degradation in Prefix-Cached Agent Serving
papers.abstract: This paper identifies a critical performance issue in serving LLM agents called "persistent degradation." The core method involves observing how prefix caching, crucial for economic serving, leads to a metastable state where even small bursts of traffic can cause a server to enter a significantly degraded performance regime, characterized by low hit ratios and reduced throughput. The main contribution is demonstrating this phenomenon and its underlying cause: the interaction between prefix caching, growing session contexts, and limited KV cache capacity, leading to prolonged performance drops.

papers.title: Can Large Language Models Develop Gambling Addiction?
papers.abstract: This paper investigates when Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit irrational, "addiction-like" gambling behavior. The core method involves manipulating LLM parameters like bet size and profit goals, revealing that increased autonomy in these areas significantly amplifies risk-taking and bankruptcy. The contribution is identifying specific conditions that induce pathological gambling patterns in LLMs and demonstrating that these behaviors can be traced to internal decision-making states.
papers.figure_caption: Two-phase study design. Phase 1. Six LLMs run the slot-machine and investment-choice tasks crossed by bet-size autonomy and goal source; round-level behavioural indicators ( I BA I_{\( \text{BA} \)} , I LC I_{\( \text{LC} \)} , I EC I_{\( \text{EC} \)} ), bankruptcy, and moving-target rates summarise the behaviour. Phase 2. SAE readouts of decision-time hidden states and cross-task PCA comparisons evaluate two open-weight models. These tests ask whether behavioural contrasts are decodable at the representational level across the three task surfaces (SM/IC/MW), whether endpoint risk shares low-rank geometry across tasks, and whether autonomy modulates how legibly each readout reads. A fourth test asks whether a direction built from the model’s own betting moves the wager. The middle panel poses the question tested in Section 4 . Per-task BK readout weights are nearly orthogonal, while the three tasks’ mean-difference BK directions share a small component (Section 4.2 ).

papers.title: Diff-Instruct with Diffused Reward: Towards Principled One-step Generator RL
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Diff-Instruct with Diffused Reward (DIDR), a novel framework for one-step text-to-image generation. DIDR addresses the reward-fidelity mismatch in previous RL methods by aligning the optimal reward distribution across all diffusion noise levels. This principled approach, derived from Integral KL minimization, naturally generates a Diffused Reward Score that guides the generator towards higher reward without sacrificing image quality.
papers.figure_caption: 1024 × 1024 1024\( \times \) 1024 images from one-step SDXL aligned via Didr . Prompts in Appendix I .

papers.title: DOTRAG: Retrieval-Time Reasoning Along Paths
papers.abstract: DotRAG addresses challenges in complex graph retrieval by using LLM reasoning to efficiently identify relevant relational paths. Its core method involves indexing the knowledge graph with a summary overview and reachability information, allowing the LLM to quickly narrow down search regions and hypothesize relationship sequences at query time. This training-free approach avoids costly online traversals and rigid heuristics, improving retrieval accuracy for complex relational tasks.
